How to write a sales follow-up email after a call

The follow-up email decides whether the next call happens. It should take two minutes to write and be impossible to misread: what you heard, who does what by when, and the one thing you still need. Here is the method, with a worked example produced from the call notes below by the free Sales Call Notes Desk.

The five rules

  1. Send it the same day. A recap three days later reads as an afterthought.
  2. Recap their problem in their words. A quoted sentence proves you listened better than any adjective.
  3. Date every next step, yours and theirs. An undated step is a hope. The tool flags a call with no dated next step.
  4. Ask for at most two things. Pick from decision maker, timeline and budget, whichever the call left blank.
  5. Add nothing you did not hear. No new price, discount or promise. A number first appearing in the recap reopens the call in writing.

Worked example

The notes (invented):

Call with Dana Reyes (Ops Director), Brightline Logistics, 45 min.
Dana: Right now dispatch builds the weekly routes by hand in spreadsheets. It takes two people about 12 hours a week and we still get errors, maybe 8% of stops are wrong.
Dana: We looked at RouteWorks last year but it was too expensive for our size.
Dana: Budget is roughly $20k a year, I'd have to check with Marcus (CFO) because he signs off on anything over $15k.
Dana: We have to be live before peak season starts on January 15.
Dana: Security review with their IT team takes about three weeks. Must have a QuickBooks integration.
Me: I'll send the sample route comparison by Tuesday.
Dana: I'll loop in Marcus and get you thirty minutes with him.
Me: I'll book a follow-up with Marcus for next Thursday.

The tool finds 9 of 9 qualification fields answered, flags no risks, and drafts this email, which you edit and send yourself:

Hi Dana,

Thanks for the time on Brightline Logistics. A quick recap so we are working from the same page.

What I heard:
- Right now dispatch builds the weekly routes by hand in spreadsheets.
- It takes two people about 12 hours a week and we still get errors, maybe 8% of stops are wrong.

What we agreed:
- I will send the sample route comparison by Tuesday (Tue, Oct 20)
- I will book a follow-up with Marcus for next Thursday (Thu, Oct 22)

On your side, as I noted it:
- “I'll loop in Marcus and get you thirty minutes with him”

Let me know if I got anything wrong.

Sam

Dates are worked out from a call on Saturday 17 October 2026. Paste your own notes to do the same, free, in your browser.

Questions

How long should a sales follow-up email be?

Under 200 words. It is read on a phone between meetings, so the recap, the agreed steps with dates and one question fit and nothing else needs to.

When should I send the follow-up email after a call?

The same day, while both sides remember the call. A recap sent three days later reads as an afterthought and gives the other side time to cool off.

Should the follow-up email include pricing?

Only a number the contact said or you both agreed on. A price that first appears in the recap reopens the call in writing. If a quote is the agreed next step, say it is coming by a date and send it separately.

What if the contact said send me some info?

Treat it as a request for a meeting, not a document. Ask what they would want to see in it and book fifteen minutes to go through it together, because a deck sent into silence is rarely read.

The model email must pass the same checks (no dollar figure that is not in your notes, no guarantees); otherwise the built-in email is kept and you are told. The key is kept only in this browser if you tick the box.

    Questions

    How do I turn sales call notes into CRM fields?

    Paste the notes or transcript and the tool reads them for pain, quantified impact, budget, decision maker, timeline, decision process, decision criteria, alternatives and a dated next step, and shows the sentence each came from. One click gives you a CSV row or a block of text to paste into the deal record. Anything the notes do not say is left blank and listed as a question for the next call, never guessed.

    What is the difference between BANT and MEDDIC?

    BANT checks four things: budget, authority, need and timeline. MEDDIC adds quantified impact, the economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, the pain and a champion, which suits longer deals with several people involved. This tool reports nine fields that cover both lists, so you can see at a glance which parts of either checklist your call actually answered.

    How do I write a good follow-up email after a sales call?

    Send it the same day, keep it under 200 words, recap the problem in the contact's own words, list what each side agreed to do with a date, and end on one clear next step. Do not add prices, discounts or promises that were not said on the call. The tool drafts exactly that from your notes and checks the draft before you send it.

    Does it use AI, and are my call notes sent anywhere?

    Only if you choose. The analysis and the built-in email work with no key, using rules in your browser, and your notes are never uploaded. If you add your own API key for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, only the notes and the draft email are sent, from your browser straight to that provider, and the model email is rejected if it contains a dollar figure that is not in your notes.

    Why did it say my deal has no decision maker?

    It looks for a title such as CFO or director together with words like signs off, approves or final say. If the notes never mention who decides, it flags the gap, because a deal with one contact and no known approver is the most common way a good call goes quiet. Add the name and title to the notes and run it again.

    Can I use it on a call transcript?

    Yes. Lines that start with a name and a colon are treated as speakers. Put your own name in the Your name box and the tool sorts next steps into yours and theirs. A transcript works best trimmed to the important parts, because the rules read every sentence.

    Yes. There is no signup, no limit and no watermark. It runs in your browser, so it costs nothing to serve, and it is MIT-licensed open source you can host yourself.
